topic: Power supplies and schematic symbols (G7A; 13 pool questions)

notes.front: What is a bleeder resistor?
notes.back: A resistor connected across a power supply's filter capacitors, used to draw a fixed discharge current.
notes.explanation: It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed, so a technician working on the supply is not caught by a lethal stored charge.
notes.example: A high-value, high-power resistor wired across the output of a linear power supply's filter capacitors.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 1 glossary: "BLEEDER RESISTOR—A resistor which is used to draw a fixed current."

notes.front: What is a power supply filter network?
notes.back: A selective network of capacitors and inductors that smooths the pulsating output of a rectifier into steady DC.
notes.explanation: It works by offering little opposition to DC while blocking or attenuating the AC ripple left over from rectification.
notes.example: A capacitor across the rectifier output, sometimes followed by a series inductor, forming a simple filter network.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 6 glossary: "FILTER—A selective network of resistors, capacitors, and inductors that offer comparatively little opposition to certain frequencies or to direct current, while blocking or attenuating other frequencies."

notes.front: What is a half-wave rectifier?
notes.back: A rectifier using only one-half of each AC cycle to change AC to pulsating DC, needing only one diode.
notes.explanation: Because it uses only half the input cycle, its ripple frequency equals the AC input frequency, and it delivers less current for a given transformer than a full-wave design.
notes.example: A single diode fed from one transformer winding, conducting only during the positive half-cycle.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "HALF-WAVE RECTIFIER—A rectifier using only one-half of each cycle to change ac to pulsating dc."

notes.front: What is a full-wave rectifier?
notes.back: A circuit that uses both positive and negative alternations of an AC input to produce DC, typically with two diodes and a center-tapped transformer.
notes.explanation: Using both halves of the cycle gives twice the ripple frequency of a half-wave rectifier and lets more current be drawn.
notes.example: Two diodes, each fed from one half of a center-tapped transformer secondary, conducting on alternate half-cycles.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "FULL-WAVE RECTIFIER—A circuit that uses both positive and negative alternations in an alternating current to produce direct current."

notes.front: What is a center-tapped transformer?
notes.back: A transformer with an extra connection at a winding's electrical midpoint, giving a full-wave rectifier's two diodes a common reference point.
notes.explanation: The center tap gives a full-wave rectifier a ground reference so each diode conducts on alternate half-cycles.
notes.example: The secondary of a full-wave rectifier's power transformer, tapped at its midpoint, feeding two diodes.

notes.front: What is a switchmode power supply?
notes.back: A power supply whose high-frequency switching operation allows the use of smaller filter components than a linear design.
notes.explanation: Running the switching element at a high frequency, rather than at the AC line frequency, lets the filter inductors and capacitors be much smaller and lighter.
notes.example: A compact laptop charger uses a switchmode design rather than a heavy 60 Hz transformer.

notes.front: What is a linear power supply?
notes.back: A power supply that rectifies and filters at the AC line frequency, regulating with a continuously conducting pass element rather than a high-frequency switch.
notes.explanation: Because it filters at the low line frequency, a linear supply needs larger, heavier filter components than a switchmode design.
notes.example: An older, heavy bench power supply built around a large mains transformer and a linear regulator.

notes.front: What is a Zener diode?
notes.back: A PN-junction diode designed to operate in the reverse-bias breakdown region, giving it a stable, predictable voltage drop there.
notes.explanation: Unlike a normal diode, which is never meant to be run in reverse breakdown, a Zener diode is specifically built to work that way as a voltage reference.
notes.example: A Zener diode setting a stable reference voltage in a simple voltage regulator circuit.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "ZENER DIODE—A PN-junction diode designed to operate in the reverse-bias breakdown region."

notes.front: What is an NPN junction transistor?
notes.back: A bipolar junction transistor built from an N-type, then P-type, then N-type semiconductor layer, one of the two basic BJT polarities.
notes.explanation: It is one of the schematic symbols identified in figure G7-1, alongside the FET, Zener diode, transformer and tapped inductor.
notes.example: An NPN transistor conducts when its base is driven positive relative to its emitter.

notes.front: What is a tapped inductor?
notes.back: An inductor with one or more additional connections partway along its winding, letting it supply more than one voltage or coupling point.
notes.explanation: It is one of the schematic symbols identified in figure G7-1.
notes.example: A tapped inductor used in an oscillator or matching network to pick off a fraction of the total inductance.

notes.front: What is a solid core transformer?
notes.back: A transformer wound on a continuous solid magnetic core, as opposed to an air core, giving it strong magnetic coupling between windings.
notes.explanation: It is one of the schematic symbols identified in figure G7-1.
notes.example: The power transformer in a linear power supply is typically a solid (laminated iron) core transformer.

notes.front: What is the function of a power supply bleeder resistor?
notes.back: It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed.
notes.explanation: This removes a shock hazard from the stored charge that would otherwise remain in the filter capacitors after switch-off.

notes.front: Which components are used in a power supply filter network?
notes.back: Capacitors and inductors.
notes.explanation: These reactive components smooth the rectifier's pulsating output into steady DC.

notes.front: How do half-wave and full-wave rectifiers differ in diodes needed, AC portion converted, and unfiltered output?
notes.back: Half-wave: one diode, converts 180°. Full-wave: two diodes and a center-tapped transformer, converts 360°, output pulses at twice the input frequency.
notes.explanation: Using both halves of the AC cycle in a full-wave design roughly doubles the ripple frequency and the current a given transformer can deliver.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G7A03, G7A04, G7A05, G7A06, G7A07

notes.front: What is the main advantage of a switchmode power supply over a linear one?
notes.back: High-frequency operation allows the use of smaller components.
notes.explanation: Filtering at a much higher frequency than the AC line lets the filter inductors and capacitors shrink dramatically.

notes.front: Which figure G7-1 symbol numbers represent the FET, NPN junction transistor, Zener diode, solid core transformer and tapped inductor?
notes.back: 1 FET; 2 NPN junction transistor; 5 Zener diode; 6 solid core transformer; 7 tapped inductor.
notes.explanation: Learning the symbol numbers, not just the symbol shapes, is what the exam actually asks for figure G7-1 questions.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G7A09, G7A10, G7A11, G7A12, G7A13

notes.front: In what region does a Zener diode operate to give a stable reference voltage?
notes.back: The reverse-bias breakdown region.
notes.explanation: An ordinary diode is never meant to be driven into reverse breakdown, but a Zener diode is specifically designed to work there without damage.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "ZENER DIODE—A PN-junction diode designed to operate in the reverse-bias breakdown region."

notes.front: What is the function of a power supply bleeder resistor?
notes.back: It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed
notes.choices:
A) It acts as a fuse for excess voltage
B) It discharges the filter capacitors when power is removed
C) It removes shock hazards from the induction coils
D) It eliminates ground loop current
notes.choicesExplained: A describes fuse behaviour, not a resistor's function. C names the wrong component (induction coils, not filter capacitors). D describes a grounding and bonding issue unrelated to a bleeder resistor.
notes.explanation: The bleeder resistor drains the stored charge from the filter capacitors after the supply is switched off.

notes.front: Which of the following components are used in a power supply filter network?
notes.back: Capacitors and inductors
notes.choices:
A) Diodes
B) Transformers and transducers
C) Capacitors and inductors
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A names the rectifier component, not the filter component. B lists devices that are not the filter network's building blocks. D is wrong because A and B are not correct, so it cannot be all of them.
notes.explanation: Capacitors and inductors, not diodes or transformers, are the reactive parts that smooth the rectified output.

notes.front: Which type of rectifier circuit uses two diodes and a center-tapped transformer?
notes.back: Full-wave
notes.choices:
A) Full-wave
B) Full-wave bridge
C) Half-wave
D) Synchronous
notes.choicesExplained: B a bridge rectifier uses four diodes and does not need a center-tapped transformer. C a half-wave rectifier needs only one diode. D (synchronous) is a rectifier that uses switching transistors, not two diodes and a center tap.
notes.explanation: The center tap gives each of the two diodes its own half of the secondary to conduct from on alternate half-cycles.

notes.front: What is characteristic of a half-wave rectifier in a power supply?
notes.back: Only one diode is required
notes.choices:
A) Only one diode is required
B) The ripple frequency is twice that of a full-wave rectifier
C) More current can be drawn from the half-wave rectifier
D) The output voltage is two times the peak input voltage
notes.choicesExplained: B reverses the relationship: a full-wave rectifier's ripple frequency is twice the half-wave's, not the other way round. C and D describe advantages a half-wave rectifier does not actually have.
notes.explanation: Using only one diode is the defining simplicity of a half-wave rectifier.

notes.front: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a half-wave rectifier?
notes.back: 180 degrees
notes.choices:
A) 90 degrees
B) 180 degrees
C) 270 degrees
D) 360 degrees
notes.choicesExplained: A is only a quarter cycle, too little. C is not a meaningful fraction of a single AC cycle here. D is the full-wave, not half-wave, figure.
notes.explanation: A half-wave rectifier conducts for only one half-cycle, 180 degrees out of the full 360.

notes.front: What portion of the AC cycle is converted to DC by a full-wave rectifier?
notes.back: 360 degrees
notes.choices:
A) 90 degrees
B) 180 degrees
C) 270 degrees
D) 360 degrees
notes.choicesExplained: B is the half-wave, not full-wave, figure. A and C are not meaningful fractions of the cycle for either rectifier type.
notes.explanation: A full-wave rectifier conducts current during both halves of the AC cycle, the entire 360 degrees.

notes.front: What is the output waveform of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier connected to a resistive load?
notes.back: A series of DC pulses at twice the frequency of the AC input
notes.choices:
A) A series of DC pulses at twice the frequency of the AC input
B) A series of DC pulses at the same frequency as the AC input
C) A sine wave at half the frequency of the AC input
D) A steady DC voltage
notes.choicesExplained: B describes a half-wave, not full-wave, rectifier's ripple frequency. C is not what an unfiltered rectifier produces. D requires a filter network, which is absent here.
notes.explanation: Both halves of the AC cycle contribute a pulse, so the pulse rate doubles compared with a half-wave rectifier.

notes.front: Which of the following is characteristic of a switchmode power supply as compared to a linear power supply?
notes.back: High-frequency operation allows the use of smaller components
notes.choices:
A) Faster switching time makes higher output voltage possible
B) Fewer circuit components are required
C) High-frequency operation allows the use of smaller components
D) Inherently more stable
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are not the recognised advantage of switchmode operation; the defining benefit is component size at high switching frequency.
notes.explanation: Filtering at a much higher frequency than the AC line lets the filter components shrink significantly.

notes.front: Which symbol in figure G7-1 represents a field effect transistor?
notes.back: Symbol 1
notes.choices:
A) Symbol 2
B) Symbol 5
C) Symbol 1
D) Symbol 4
notes.choicesExplained: A (symbol 2) is the NPN junction transistor. B (symbol 5) is the Zener diode. D (symbol 4) is not the FET in this figure.
notes.explanation: Figure G7-1 numbers each symbol; symbol 1 is keyed to the field effect transistor.

notes.front: How do half-wave and full-wave rectifiers differ in diode count, degrees converted and ripple frequency?
notes.back: Half-wave: one diode, 180°, ripple at the input frequency. Full-wave: two diodes plus a center-tapped transformer, 360°, ripple at twice the input frequency.
notes.explanation: Mixing up which one doubles the ripple frequency is the most common way to miss a rectifier question.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G7A04, G7A05, G7A06, G7A07

notes.front: How do switchmode and linear power supplies differ in filtering frequency and component size?
notes.back: Switchmode filters at a high switching frequency, allowing small components; linear filters at the AC line frequency and needs larger, heavier components.
notes.explanation: The two designs trade complexity for size differently, and the exam tests only this size-versus-frequency relationship.

notes.front: How does a Zener diode differ from an ordinary rectifier diode in its intended use?
notes.back: A rectifier diode conducts only in forward bias; a Zener diode is built to run in reverse-bias breakdown as a stable voltage reference.
notes.explanation: Running an ordinary diode into reverse breakdown usually destroys it, but that is exactly the region a Zener diode is built to work in.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "ZENER DIODE—A PN-junction diode designed to operate in the reverse-bias breakdown region."
